espinha: As três camadas do contrato da pauta (§3), entre uma régua e uma cena: a régua (p1: o que o censo contou e o contorno do distrito), a terra (p2–p3), a história (p4–p6), o hoje (p7–p8) e o fecho no mirante de Bixby Creek (p9). A cada camada, cada número diz de que contorno é (o distrito, a costa do plano, 1986, 2020, a pesquisa de 5 anos). Dois fios atravessam as partes: o PLANO DE 1986 como personagem (o clima, os limites, os anos 1880, a estrada, a regra, os trabalhadores) e a PONTE DE BIXBY (a 1ª imagem; 'the census district around this bridge'; o nome do colono em p4; a travessia da estrada em p5; o mirante que a regra nomeia em p6; o fecho em p9). Dois fios visuais: o POLÍGONO DO DISTRITO aceso a cada número dele (e a costa do plano em tracejado próprio a cada número dela) e o PERFIL DA ENCOSTA, do 'a estrada' (a serra caindo no mar com a estrada como uma prateleira a meia altura), que volta em p2 (o chão que falta), p5 (as explosões) e p7 (a encosta que desliza e as barras de aço). A virada final é a da régua (p8): contado por moradores, é o Wyoming; por casas e por carros, a costa não é vazia.
resumo: Big Sur fica entre Los Angeles e San Francisco, cujas regiões metropolitanas somam mais de 17 milhões; o distrito do censo em volta da ponte de Bixby contou menos de 1.500 pessoas em 2020, tão vazio quanto o Wyoming. Não é o clima (o plano de 1986 o chama de ameno), e não é que ninguém veio (quase mil nos anos 1880, na costa do plano). O distrito cobre dois terços da costa (o sul é outro distrito); umas seis pessoas por milha quadrada, como o Wyoming, num estado mais de 40 vezes mais cheio. A terra: a serra de Santa Lucia sobe a 5.200 pés e cai no mar, sem chão para cidade nem porto; o plano lista água, acesso, solo instável, fogo e enchente; só uma outra estrada, pela serra; água pouca e sazonal; metade da área do plano é floresta nacional e área selvagem; e a terra anda (Mud Creek, 2017, filmado por Shawn Harrison, do USGS). A história: gado, sequoia, casca, cal e ouro, tudo por mar; Notley's Landing e Manchester; a estrada perigosa que fechava parte do ano, o único freio do turismo no sul, pelo plano; a ideia de Doctor John Roberts; a obra de 1919 (FHWA) a junho de 1937 (US$ 8 milhões, o plano), com presos de três acampamentos de San Quentin a 35 centavos por dia; a venda de John Pfeiffer em 1934, o começo da proteção; 'A way of life had ended'; a estrada de passagem, a primeira 'scenic highway' do estado em 1965, o tráfego de verão quase todo de recreação. A resposta do condado em 1986: metade pública, a regra do que se vê da estrada e dos mirantes (o teste da visão normal, em qualquer direção, por qualquer tempo, em qualquer estação; o mirante de Bixby Creek entre os nomeados), as casas novas escondidas pela terra ou pelas árvores, a estrada racionada (quase três milhões de visitantes, o dobro esperado, no máximo 15 % para as casas novas); a regra não esvaziou a costa: decidiu como ela se vê e para quem é a estrada. O hoje: Paul's Slide e Regent's Slide, quase três anos sem atravessar a costa, a reabertura de 14/01/2026 (quase US$ 83 milhões), o Timber Fire de agosto de 2026 (centenas de casas e prédios ameaçados, trechos fechados dentro do distrito por semanas), a estrada aberta em novembro de 2026; quase quatro em dez casas vazias no dia do censo, quase todas de uso ocasional pela pesquisa do Census Bureau (um terço na Califórnia); os trabalhadores de 1986 sem casa; os visitantes que voltaram e seguem viagem. O vazio depende do que se conta. O fecho volta ao mirante de Bixby Creek: quase nenhuma casa à vista, em parte pela serra, em parte por uma escolha de 1986, entre as duas metrópoles.
pergunta: Why is the census district around Big Sur, on the coast between Los Angeles and San Francisco, as empty as Wyoming, when people already lived along this coast in the 1880s?
pergunta_no_gancho: Duas, curtas: 'Why?' (S4: palavra 35 do texto, 36 da cópia para a voz com '1,500' = 'fifteen hundred', 14,4 s a 150 palavras/min, 11,7 s a 184) e 'So why didn't more follow?' (S9, a segunda virada: palavra ~79 da voz, ~32 s a 150). A segunda é a pergunta do gancho para o portão (a última frase com '?' antes da assinatura); nenhuma sequência de 5 palavras dela volta no fecho.
pergunta_longa: Why does a stretch of coast between Los Angeles and San Francisco hold a census district as empty as Wyoming, if people were already living there in the 1880s?

tese.frase: O distrito do censo de Big Sur tem a densidade do Wyoming não pelo clima nem por falta de quem viesse, mas porque três camadas se somam, cada uma medida pelo seu dono: a terra deixa pouco lugar para morar (a serra que cai no mar, o solo que desliza, a água pouca e sazonal, e metade da área do plano em floresta nacional e área selvagem); a história fez da costa um lugar de passagem (quase mil pessoas viviam do que mandavam por mar nos anos 1880; a estrada só ficou pronta em 1937, e trouxe visitantes; o plano do condado de 1986 proibiu o novo que se vê da Highway 1 e guardou a maior parte da estrada para a recreação); e o hoje mantém o padrão (a estrada fechada por quase três anos e de novo no fogo de 2026, casas que existem e ficam vazias, quase todas de uso ocasional, e visitantes que voltam e seguem viagem). O vazio é um vazio de moradores: contado por casas ou por carros, esta costa não é vazia.
o_que_ela_nao_diz: que a regra de 1986 criou o vazio: a costa já era pouco povoada antes (p6 b8: 'The rule didn't empty this coast')
que a população não cresceu desde os anos 1880, que é 'a mesma' ou que é menor: os quase mil são da costa do plano, e o 1.474 é de parte dela
que construir é proibido: só o novo que se vê da estrada e dos mirantes; o resto, com condições (p6 b6)
que a regra vale igual hoje (pauta §11, item 2)
que ninguém mora lá, ou que é 'a cidade de Big Sur' (p1 b1 diz que o censo não conta uma cidade com esse nome)
que a estrada é a única causa, ou o assunto do vídeo (pauta §9: a estrada é um dos três porquês, nunca o assunto)
que a Highway 1 é a única estrada (p2 b4 diz o contrário)
que o fogo destruiu casas, ou qualquer número do fogo na voz
que as casas vazias são de ricos, mansões ou casas de bilionários; o preço das casas
que é a costa mais vazia da Califórnia, ou o plano mais rígido do país
que a regra tirou de vista as casas antigas: ela regula o que é novo

promessa: Explicar por que um pedaço da costa da Califórnia, entre as regiões metropolitanas de Los Angeles e de San Francisco (mais de 17 milhões), tem um distrito do censo com menos de 1.500 pessoas, tão vazio quanto o Wyoming, se não é o clima e se já havia gente nesta costa nos anos 1880; e mostrar o que esse 'vazio' mede.

payoff.resposta: A terra (p2–p3): a serra que cai no mar, sem chão para cidade nem porto, os limites que o plano lista, uma só outra estrada, a água pouca e sazonal, metade da área do plano pública e a terra que anda. A história (p4–p6): a gente dos anos 1880 vivia pelo mar; a estrada chegou tarde (1919–1937, com presos), acabou com um modo de vida e trouxe gente de passagem; o plano de 1986 proibiu o novo que se vê da estrada, mandou as casas novas para trás da terra e das árvores e guardou a estrada para os visitantes. O hoje (p7–p8): a estrada que fecha (2023–2026; o fogo de 2026), as casas que existem e ficam vazias, quase todas de uso ocasional, e os visitantes que voltam e seguem. A virada da régua (p8): contado por moradores, é o Wyoming; por casas e por carros, não. O fecho (p9) diz a resposta numa cena: do mirante que a regra nomeia, quase nenhuma casa à vista, 'Part of that is the mountains, and part of it was a choice.'
payoff.texto_previsto_em_ingles: Back at Bixby Creek, drivers pull into the turnout to look at the bridge from the start of this video. It's one of the viewpoints the county's rule was written to protect. The creek below carries a homesteader's name. Above it runs a road that prisoners helped cut into the cliffs. Hardly a house is in sight. Part of that is the mountains, and part of it was a choice. In 1986, the county wrote that whatever came next should stay out of this view. That highway runs all the way from one metro area to the other. Together, they hold more than 17 million people. In between, on census day, the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500 people who called it home.
payoff.onde: p9, a cena no mirante de Bixby Creek, sem repetir a pergunta do gancho e sem lista.

gancho.texto:
This is Big Sur, between Los Angeles and San Francisco. Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people. But the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500, as empty as Wyoming. Why?

It isn't the weather. Monterey County's 1986 plan for this coast calls the climate mild. And it isn't that nobody came. The same plan says nearly a thousand people lived along this coast by the 1880s. So why didn't more follow? The mountains are only part of it. The rest is a road that has closed again and again, and a rule in that plan about building in sight of it. And then there are the homes that often sit empty. You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the coast that never filled up begins.

The census doesn't count a town called Big Sur. It counts a district, one of the areas the Census Bureau draws inside a county to report its numbers. This one, in Monterey County, carries the name Big Sur.

It begins a few miles south of Carmel and follows the shore past this bridge, far down the coast. Behind the shore, it climbs into the mountains. Altogether, it takes in roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast. The southern end belongs to a different district, one that reaches over the mountains to a valley inland.

Wyoming had about the same that year. Among US states, only Alaska had fewer people for its size. California, the most populous state in the US, was more than 40 times as crowded.

The county's plan for this coast draws a longer outline. It covers the whole coast, more than 70 miles, from Carmel down to the next county. Keep both outlines in mind, because they don't describe the same ground. To see why the census number is so low, start with the ground itself.

partes.titulo: Mountains that drop into the sea
partes.funcao: demonstrar o primeiro mecanismo (ato 1, a física): a serra que cai no mar e as falésias, sem chão para cidade nem porto; a lista dos limites do plano (a água, o acesso, o solo instável, o fogo e a enchente); o acesso por uma estrada e meia; a água pouca e sazonal. Paga o 'It isn't the weather' do gancho e planta o fogo para p7.
partes.abre_com: o relevo da serra de Santa Lucia, com o Cone Peak ao sul do polígono do distrito (que continua aceso, mais fraco)
partes.ponte_entrada: So what makes this ground so hard to live on?
beats: b1 · A pergunta do ato 1 e a serra: 'So what makes this ground so hard to live on? Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea.' (P [53]; o Cone Peak fica no distrito de San Ardo (L1): 'near the southern end of the coast', nunca 'district' na frase ([cone-peak]).)

b2 · As falésias e o chão (do 'estrada'): 'Much of the coast is bounded by sheer cliffs, it adds, and beaches are few. That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.' (P [54], [56]; a 2ª frase é a leitura da pauta §7 do 'drop precipitously'.)
b3 · A frase-mãe: 'The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.' (P [71]; o fogo plantado para p7.)

b4 · O acesso: 'Take access. Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route into the area. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one was a lightly used county road that climbed over the mountains and crossed a military reservation.' (P [1291]: 'the basic access route to the area'; P [1293]: a Nacimiento–Fergusson, 'a lightly-used County road crossing the Hunter-Liggett Military Reservation'. É o contrário de 'the only road'. Conserto: 'That one is' → 'That one was' (a leitura é de 1986).)

b5 · A água: 'Then there's water, which sounds like the odd one out. Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal, shared by the animals, the plants and the people. Winters, it says, bring some of the heaviest rainfall in California, and summers are long and dry.' (P; P [188]; P [66], do 'estrada'. Conserto: sai o 'There's plenty of it running in the wet months' do 'vazio' (pauta §4.2: nunca 'plenty of water'); a chuva e a seca entram nas palavras do plano.)

b6 · O clima volta: 'The weather itself, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile.' (paga o 'It isn't the weather' do gancho; 'one reason', nunca 'the reason'.)
b7 · Ponte: 'The other reasons have more to do with who owns the land, and what happened on it.'
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que a serra cai direto no mar, entre falésias e quase sem praia, e não sobra chão plano; que o próprio plano do condado lista os limites (água, acesso, solo, fogo e enchente); que só havia a Highway 1 e uma estrada de serra para chegar; que há riacho, mas pouca água o ano todo; e que o clima ameno não é o problema. É uma razão, não a única.
partes.mapa: O relevo da serra de Santa Lucia: 3D com o ok do Lucas para a MapTiler deste vídeo (nenhum vale ainda); sem ele, o satélite plano com o perfil desenhado. O Cone Peak marcado ao sul do polígono do distrito; a Highway 1 (OSM) e a estrada Nacimiento–Fergusson cruzando a serra até a reserva militar (Hunter Liggett, rotulada com '1986'), as duas acesas no 'Take access'. Os riachos acesos no inverno e quase apagados no verão, no beat da água. O distrito acende inteiro no 'census district' do fim.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
So what makes this ground so hard to live on? Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea. Much of the coast is bounded by sheer cliffs, it adds, and beaches are few. That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.

The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.

Take access. Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route into the area. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one was a lightly used county road that climbed over the mountains and crossed a military reservation.

Then there's water, which sounds like the odd one out. Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal, shared by the animals, the plants and the people. Winters, it says, bring some of the heaviest rainfall in California, and summers are long and dry.

The weather itself, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile. The other reasons have more to do with who owns the land, and what happened on it.

partes.funcao: complicar: metade da terra do plano é floresta nacional e área selvagem, dos EUA; os parques ficam com mais; as casas se espremem no que sobra; e a terra que sobra anda (Mud Creek, 2017, fora do distrito, com o pesquisador do USGS). Planta Paul's Slide e Regent's Slide para p7 e fecha o ato com a virada para a história.

beats: b1 · A metade pública: 'About half of the land in the county's plan lies inside the Los Padres National Forest and the Ventana Wilderness. It's federal land, owned by the US Forest Service, the plan notes.' (P [79]; P [2880]: 'Forest Service owns 75,000 acres in the Big Sur Coast Planning Unit--roughly one half the total area'. Conserto: 'run by the federal government, not lots for sale' vira a posse que o plano diz.)

b2 · O que é 'wilderness': 'A wilderness area is land set aside to stay wild, without roads or new buildings. People can hike there, but they can't move in.' (fora do dossiê: conhecimento geral, o verificador confere; a forma fraca, se ele pedir: 'The plan describes trails and backpacking camps there, not homes.' (P [2228]).)

b3 · Os parques e o que sobra: 'State parks take up more of the coast, with names like Andrew Molera and Julia Pfeiffer Burns. Homes have to fit on what's left, and much of what's left is steep.' (P [1236]–[1239]. Conserto: sai o 'In 1986, the plan named the main pockets of homes and shops: the Big Sur River valley, Lucia and Gorda...' do 'vazio' (o plano diz 'significant residential use' em P [1537], e Gorda fica fora do distrito).)

b4 · A terra que anda: 'And the ground itself can move. In 2017, at a place called Mud Creek, a whole hillside slid down over the highway. Mud Creek lies near the southern end of the coast, outside the census district.' (L6; pauta §4.2 ('a whole hillside', o tamanho não se diz); L1: Mud Creek no distrito de San Ardo, dito na voz, do 'estrada'.)

b5 · Shawn Harrison: 'That July, Shawn Harrison, a researcher with the US Geological Survey, flew a drone over the slide. The agency was tracking how the slide kept changing. In his video, the road simply disappears under a new slope of earth and rock.' (L6: o vídeo de 19/07/2017; 'changing landslide', o título da página.)

b6 · A planta para p7: 'Mud Creek wasn't the end of it. Caltrans, California's highway department, has names for other slopes that have closed the road since then. Two of them, Paul's Slide and Regent's Slide, will matter later in this story.' (L5; 'wasn't the end of it' no lugar do 'wasn't the last time' do 'vazio' (o alerta 'last' sai); as datas ficam para p7, e o ponto de cada um, para o mapista (K4).)
b7 · Ponte: 'Steep ground, slipping ground, public ground, and not much water. Even so, long before the highway, people made a living on this coast.'

About half of the land in the county's plan lies inside the Los Padres National Forest and the Ventana Wilderness. It's federal land, owned by the US Forest Service, the plan notes. State parks take up more of the coast, with names like Andrew Molera and Julia Pfeiffer Burns. Homes have to fit on what's left, and much of what's left is steep.

And the ground itself can move. In 2017, at a place called Mud Creek, a whole hillside slid down over the highway. Mud Creek lies near the southern end of the coast, outside the census district. That July, Shawn Harrison, a researcher with the US Geological Survey, flew a drone over the slide. The agency was tracking how the slide kept changing. In his video, the road simply disappears under a new slope of earth and rock.

Mud Creek wasn't the end of it. Caltrans, California's highway department, has names for other slopes that have closed the road since then. Two of them, Paul's Slide and Regent's Slide, will matter later in this story.

Steep ground, slipping ground, public ground, and not much water. Even so, long before the highway, people made a living on this coast.

partes.titulo: The rule about what you can see
partes.funcao: virar: a resposta do condado em 1986. Metade da zona costeira já era pública; a regra do que se vê ('critical viewshed'), com o mirante de Bixby Creek entre os nomeados e o teste da visão nas palavras do plano; as casas novas fora da vista, escondidas pela terra ou pelas árvores; e a estrada tratada como recurso escasso, guardada para a recreação, com as casas novas limitadas a 15 %. The plan also treated the road itself as a limited resource. In 1986, it counted nearly three million visitors a year. Traffic jams on Highway 1 were already a problem, the plan says. It expected the number of visitors to double. So it reserved most of the highway's capacity for recreation and visitors. All the new homes together could use no more than 15 percent of it.

The rule didn't empty this coast. The coast was thinly settled long before 1986. What the plan decided was how the coast should look from the road, and who the road was for. In the 2020s, the trouble was keeping that road open at all.

destino_das_cifras.cortar_primeiro: Se o roteiro passar de 2.450 ou ficar denso: (1) a frase dos Post (p4 b3, ~23 palavras); (2) Manchester (p4 b5, O2, ~36); (3) 'California voters approved more state money for it soon after.' (p5, 10); (4) 'Other families, after the Pfeiffers, had given land for parks too, and the plan credits their generosity.' (p6, 17); (5) 'Air tankers from across California flew missions over the ridges.' (p7, 10). Nunca abaixo de 2.250; o gancho e o fecho não se cortam.
destino_das_cifras.crescer: Se o roteiro ficar abaixo de 2.250, as reservas, todas lidas na cópia local do plano ou nas leituras da Sala: p2 (as enxurradas, sem o 1972), p4 (Rockland Landing e o fim do calcário), p5 (os visitantes de outros estados e países), p6 (o 'marginal effects'), p7 (os metros cúbicos de terra de Regent's). Cada uma está no campo 'crescer' da parte.

presenca.regra: Presença humana é a pessoa ou o grupo que o dossiê documenta, num lugar e num tempo, com o que a fonte diz e nada mais; nunca inventada nem composta. O que falta fica declarado.
presenca.a_principal: Os colonos que deram nome ao mapa, num laço entre p4 e o fecho: Charlie Bixby (a ponte do gancho e o riacho do fecho), os Pfeiffer (John Pfeiffer, que em 1934 vendeu terra ao estado para o núcleo do Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park, o começo da proteção segundo o plano; e os parques), Jim Anderson e os Post (o rancho onde ficaram o correio original e a segunda escola de Big Sur). Fonte: o plano de 1986 (P [1203], [1218]–[1221], [1235]).
as_outras: Godfrey Notley e o povoado de Notley's Landing, no tempo dos desembarcadouros (P [1206]–[1207]); Manchester, a cidade do ouro de Alder Creek, que começou a minguar em 1895 (P [1213]–[1216], opcional).
Os moradores que, na virada do século, guiavam caçadores e pescadores das cidades, e os primeiros visitantes, de diligência (P [1485]–[1487]).
Doctor John Roberts, fundador de Seaside, de quem veio a ideia da estrada aberta o ano todo (P [1227]–[1228]).

Os presos dos três acampamentos de San Quentin (Little Sur River, Kirk Creek e, depois, Anderson Creek), a 35 centavos por dia e com a pena reduzida (FHWA, L4); sem nomes e sem o ano de chegada. Voltam no fecho ('prisoners helped cut').
Os colonos furiosos com as explosões nas encostas (P [1229]–[1231]).
Quem trabalhava na costa em 1986, sobretudo para os visitantes, e às vezes acampava, dormia no carro ou ia morar com amigos (P [1547]–[1548]).
Shawn Harrison, pesquisador do USGS, que filmou Mud Creek com drone em 19/07/2017 (L6).

As equipes da Caltrans em Regent's Slide (as barras de aço); em 2026, os bombeiros feridos e os aviões-tanque de todo o estado no Timber Fire, e a gente que vive ao longo da estrada, que passou pelo fogo logo depois dos deslizamentos (DS2, K1).
presenca.o_que_falta: Não há morador de hoje com nome, nem relato em primeira pessoa dos anos sem estrada ou do fogo; as evacuações de 2026 são só da busca (fora). Não há foto com licença dos presos nem dos colonos (a conferir). Não se sabe o ano em que os presos chegaram nem quem fez a ponte de Bixby, e quando (pauta §11, itens 3 e 4). O roteiro não inventa nada disso.

avisos_dos_leitores.o distrito claro no mapa (o 1.474 é só p: A voz aponta o distrito na frase da surpresa ('the census district around this bridge') e o p1 o define ('The census doesn't count a town called Big Sur. It counts a district...'), diz por onde ele vai, 'roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast', 'The southern end belongs to a different district', e dá a segunda régua (a costa do plano, mais de 70 milhas). O polígono do TIGER 2020 acende a cada número do distrito (gancho, p1, p2, p7, p8, p9); a costa do plano tem o tracejado próprio quando um número dela é dito (gancho, p1, p4); Mud Creek é dito 'outside the census district'. A miniatura 'ONLY 1,474' só é honesta com o polígono (o cético).
avisos_dos_leitores.a virada além de 'é montanha' ou 'é parq: O gancho já diz 'The mountains are only part of it' e anuncia a estrada, a regra e as casas vazias. No corpo: a gente dos anos 1880, vivendo pelo mar, e a estrada perigosa que segurava o turismo (p4); a estrada que acabou com um modo de vida e trouxe gente de passagem (p5); a regra do que se vê, com o mirante da ponte, o teste da visão e as casas escondidas, e a estrada guardada para a recreação, com as casas novas a 15 % (p6); as casas que existem e ficam vazias, quase todas de uso ocasional, e os trabalhadores sem casa (p8); a virada da régua (p8); e o fecho, 'Part of that is the mountains, and part of it was a choice' (p9).
avisos_dos_leitores.os turistas entram: Em seis partes: o turismo que a estrada perigosa segurava, os visitantes de diligência e os guias de caça (p4); a estrada a menos de um dia de carro das metrópoles, a 'scenic highway' de 1965 e o tráfego de verão quase todo de recreação (p5); os quase três milhões por ano de 1986, os engarrafamentos e a estrada guardada para eles (p6); 'the visitors came back' em 2026 e 'Then they drive on. The census doesn't count them' (p8); 'Count the cars on Highway 1' (p8); e os motoristas no mirante (p9).

fecho.forma: uma cena num lugar do mapa: o mirante de Bixby Creek, que o plano de 1986 nomeia, ao lado da ponte da abertura, terminando no mapa com as duas metrópoles e o distrito
fecho.nao_repete_a_pergunta: Nenhuma sequência de 5 palavras de 'So why didn't more follow?' nas 8 últimas frases; nem 'So' nem pergunta no fecho; o 'Why?' não volta. O portão rodado no esqueleto não deu alerta de fecho.
fecho.nao_e_lista: Nenhuma das 8 últimas frases abre com First, Then, Next, Finally, Second, A ou An; a resposta vem numa cena e numa frase ('Part of that is the mountains, and part of it was a choice'). O tríptico 'Count … Count … Count …' fica em p8, fora das 8 últimas frases, e é a régua, não a lista de causas.
fecho.como_paga: Paga o título (a última frase volta a 'the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500', entre as duas metrópoles de mais de 17 milhões) e a pergunta do gancho ('Why?' e 'why didn't more follow?': a serra e uma escolha de 1986, ditas sobre a vista que a regra protege), sem repeti-la.
fecho.contra_os_anteriores: Juneau, Los Angeles, a Zona do Canal e o Peru fecharam com 'So', a pergunta repetida, a resposta em lista e uma imagem curta (voz §1); o Atlântico fechou num fato atribuído dito como imagem de lugar (a borda dos peixes). Este fecha numa cena de mirante com um documento (o plano que nomeia o mirante) e as duas cifras do gancho espelhadas.

inscricao.onde: fim de p4, sobre 'Some locals earned extra money guiding hunters and fishermen from the cities. A road you could count on in every season was decades away.' e a pausa de parágrafo antes de p5.
inscricao.depois_de: guiding hunters and fishermen from the cities.
inscricao.fala_curta_prevista: A road you could count on in every season was decades away. (12 palavras, sem 'here' nem 'this line', sem número-herói nem frase-chave)
inscricao.posicao_estimada: termina na palavra 1111 de 2379 (≈ 6:02 de fala a 184, num vídeo de ≈ 13:20 com a vinheta e a cauda: ~46 %; a 150, ≈ 7:24 de ≈ 16:16: ~46 %): dentro de 35–60 % e fora do 1º minuto (cta §6).
inscricao.por_que: Frase calma, sem número, fora da frase-chave da parte (que é a dos quase mil e a régua do plano), sobre o mapa da costa do plano já pousado, com os desembarcadouros acesos e a estrada antiga em pontilhado, câmera parada; nenhum território acendendo nem número-herói no trecho. Se a regência puser ali uma foto de época (pauta §6, item 5), melhor: registro parado.
inscricao.reserva: p3 b5, sobre 'The agency was tracking how the slide kept changing.' (~37 %), só com o drone do USGS parado e o canto livre; nunca sobre a encosta deslizando.
inscricao.nao_ali: o gancho e o 1º minuto; p1 b3–b4 (a régua desenhada); p5 b1–b3 (a linha do tempo e os acampamentos acendendo); p6 (a regra, o cone de visão, o mirante acendendo); p7 (os fechamentos animados).

comentario.onde: p9 b2, sobre 'The creek below carries a homesteader's name. Above it runs a road that prisoners helped cut into the cliffs.' (~20 palavras: ~8 s a 150, ~6,5 s a 184), lugar=cima, com a foto da ponte por baixo, parada. É depois do último fato novo (p8): as frases de b2 só lembram p4 e p5. A peça sai antes de 'Hardly a house is in sight.' (a fala aponta a imagem) e muito antes da cauda de 20 s (cta §6). Se a voz ficar perto de 184 e a peça não couber, a saída é a do vídeo 2 (a tela final, à esquerda), que volta ao Lucas.
comentario.pergunta: Would you live in Big Sur, or just visit?
alternativas: Would you live on this coast, or just visit?
Would you live where the road can close for years? (do 'estrada'; pressupõe o 'almost three years' da Caltrans, L5: passa pelo verificador como texto de tela)
comentario.por_que: Liga-se à virada do vídeo (moradores contra visitantes), é respondível por quem acabou de ver e só oferece uma escolha (não afirma fato). Calma, em segunda pessoa, sem like, emoji nem 'smash' (cta §7).
comentario.o_que_o_roteirista_faz: Deixa as duas frases de p9 b2 calmas e sem número. Quem fecha a pergunta e a roda no 'node marca/cta/pecas/_perguntas.mjs --q="…"' é o redator-de-tela; a mesma pergunta vai à descrição e ao comentário fixado. A chamada é só de tela: a voz não a lê.

riscos.risco: O 1.500 lido como a costa inteira.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: O 1.500 só aparece duas vezes, as duas com 'the census district' na frase; o p1 não diz o 1.500, e as 70 milhas ficam no último parágrafo dele; o mapa acende o polígono a cada número do distrito.

riscos.regra: a Sala; pauta §5; [anos-1880]; o portão diz que a montagem é do verificador
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: 'nearly a thousand' sempre atribuído ao plano e dito da costa; p4 b2 diz a régua em voz; nenhuma frase compara 1880 com hoje. A pergunta 'So why didn't more follow?' é pergunta, não afirmação, e a pauta §5 manda pôr os dois na mesma cena, cada um com o dono; se o verificador ler montagem, a troca pronta é 'So why didn't more people move in?' (o mesmo tamanho; o 'Why?' não muda).

riscos.risco: As metrópoles com a régua errada.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: 'Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people' (vale em 2025 e na base de 2020); a tela diz o ano; nunca 'largest'.

riscos.risco: O Wyoming de outro ano, e a reescrita do 'menos denso'.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: 'The count is from 2020' e 'Wyoming had about the same that year'; 'Among US states, only Alaska had fewer people for its size' reescreve o 'menos denso dos 48 contíguos' (o Havaí é denso): o verificador confere, com a contagem do censo do Wyoming (K7).

riscos.risco: A regra de 1986 dita como de hoje.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: Todos os verbos da regra no passado, o teste da visão incluído ('was'); o gancho diz 'a rule in that plan about building in sight of it', sem verbo no presente; nenhum 'still', 'today', 'now', 'since 1986'.

'prohibit all future development, public or private, visible from Highway 1 and from major public viewpoints' e 'Out of sight of the road, new homes were possible, with conditions', com as condições ditas.
'Part of the labor came from prisoners', os três acampamentos, os 35 centavos e a pena reduzida, tudo da FHWA; 'prisoners helped cut' no fecho; nunca 'built by prisoners'.

O fogo em palavras, com o CAL FIRE e a Caltrans como donos; o Plaskett só pelo nome; a frase do tom ('For the people who live along this road...'); 'In August 2026' no lugar de 'last summer' (voz §2: data absoluta; o portão alerta 'last').

riscos.risco: A estrada dita fechada no presente.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: Os fechamentos no passado, com data; 'By November 2026, the road was open from end to end again' é volátil: relê-se na Caltrans antes da publicação.

riscos.risco: As casas: as duas réguas e o 'second home'.
riscos.como_o_plano_respeita: Cada régua com o dono ('On census day in 2020'; 'The Census Bureau also runs a longer survey. Its results for 2020 to 2024...'); nenhuma margem na voz; 'homes people keep, but don't live in' é a paráfrase; o O4 (1976) saiu.

riscos.risco: Os visitantes de hoje com número.

esqueleto_medido.texto:
This is Big Sur, between Los Angeles and San Francisco. Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people. But the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500, as empty as Wyoming. Why?

It isn't the weather. Monterey County's 1986 plan for this coast calls the climate mild. And it isn't that nobody came. The same plan says nearly a thousand people lived along this coast by the 1880s. So why didn't more follow? The mountains are only part of it. The rest is a road that has closed again and again, and a rule in that plan about building in sight of it. And then there are the homes that often sit empty. You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the coast that never filled up begins.

The census doesn't count a town called Big Sur. It counts a district, one of the areas the Census Bureau draws inside a county to report its numbers. This one, in Monterey County, carries the name Big Sur.

It begins a few miles south of Carmel and follows the shore past this bridge, far down the coast. Behind the shore, it climbs into the mountains. Altogether, it takes in roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast. The southern end belongs to a different district, one that reaches over the mountains to a valley inland.

The count is from 2020, the most recent census. The district has about 250 square miles of land. Spread its people across all of it. You get about six people per square mile. Wyoming had about the same that year. Among US states, only Alaska had fewer people for its size. California, the most populous state in the US, was more than 40 times as crowded.

The county's plan for this coast draws a longer outline. It covers the whole coast, more than 70 miles, from Carmel down to the next county. Keep both outlines in mind, because they don't describe the same ground. To see why the census number is so low, start with the ground itself.

So what makes this ground so hard to live on? Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea. Much of the coast is bounded by sheer cliffs, it adds, and beaches are few. That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.

The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.

Take access. Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route into the area. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one was a lightly used county road that climbed over the mountains and crossed a military reservation.

Then there's water, which sounds like the odd one out. Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal, shared by the animals, the plants and the people. Winters, it says, bring some of the heaviest rainfall in California, and summers are long and dry.

The weather itself, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile. The other reasons have more to do with who owns the land, and what happened on it.

About half of the land in the county's plan lies inside the Los Padres National Forest and the Ventana Wilderness. It's federal land, owned by the US Forest Service, the plan notes. A wilderness area is land set aside to stay wild, without roads or new buildings. People can hike there, but they can't move in. State parks take up more of the coast, with names like Andrew Molera and Julia Pfeiffer Burns. Homes have to fit on what's left, and much of what's left is steep.

And the ground itself can move. In 2017, at a place called Mud Creek, a whole hillside slid down over the highway. Mud Creek lies near the southern end of the coast, outside the census district. That July, Shawn Harrison, a researcher with the US Geological Survey, flew a drone over the slide. The agency was tracking how the slide kept changing. In his video, the road simply disappears under a new slope of earth and rock.

Mud Creek wasn't the end of it. Caltrans, California's highway department, has names for other slopes that have closed the road since then. Two of them, Paul's Slide and Regent's Slide, will matter later in this story.

Steep ground, slipping ground, public ground, and not much water. Even so, long before the highway, people made a living on this coast.

They ranched, mostly to feed their own families. They cut redwoods for lumber, and peeled tanbark, a bark used to make tannic acid. They mined limestone and gold. By the 1880s, the county's plan says, nearly a thousand people lived along this coast, mostly this way. That count is for the whole coast in the plan, not just the census district.

Some of the original homesteaders left their names on the map: the Pfeiffers, Charlie Bixby, Jim Anderson. The bridge at the start of this video carries Bixby's name. Big Sur's original post office and its second schoolhouse were built on the ranch of another homesteading family, the Posts.

There was no highway. The plan says the mountains, the deep canyons and the lack of roads made travel slow and difficult. So most of what the coast produced went out by sea. Small trading boats called at landings along the shore. They loaded lumber, bark and limestone, and they dropped off supplies. Around one of them, Notley's Landing, a thriving village grew up.

Toward the southern end, gold turned up near Alder Creek. A boomtown called Manchester sprang up, with stores, saloons, a dance hall and a hotel. By 1895, the plan says, the boom had begun to fade.

Over land, there was a road of sorts. The plan calls it hazardous, and says it had to be closed part of the year. In the plan's telling, that road was the one thing holding back tourism on the south coast. Around the turn of the century, visitors could already reach the Big Sur Valley by stagecoach from Monterey, to camp in the redwoods. Some locals earned extra money guiding hunters and fishermen from the cities. A road you could count on in every season was decades away.

The idea of a scenic highway, open all year, came from Doctor John Roberts, the founder of the city of Seaside. Work on the coast highway began in 1919, according to the Federal Highway Administration. California voters approved more state money for it soon after.

Along the route, dozens of streams had cut deep canyons to the sea, and the road had to get across each one. One of those crossings is the bridge at Bixby Creek.

Part of the labor came from prisoners. San Quentin, a California state prison, set up three temporary camps along the route. One stood by the Little Sur River, one at Kirk Creek, and later one at Anderson Creek. The inmates were paid 35 cents a day, and their sentences were reduced.

Machinery blasted through the cliffs. Many of the original settlers, the county's plan says, were enraged by the damage. It describes scarred headlands, and canyons and waterfalls fouled with debris.

In 1934, while the road was being built, John Pfeiffer sold land to the state for a park. The county's plan marks that sale as the start of the coast's long-term protection.

The highway was finished in June 1937, for about 8 million dollars, the plan says. It sums up the change in one line. A way of life had ended.

The new road put the coast within easy reach. Decades later, the county's plan noted that the Bay Area and Los Angeles were less than a day's drive away. Along the road grew campgrounds, lodges, restaurants and places to pull over for the view. In 1965, the plan notes, this stretch became California's first official scenic highway. By the 1980s, nearly all summer traffic on it was recreational, by the plan's estimate. More visitors raised a harder question for the county, about how much of this coast should be built on at all.

The county's answer came in 1986, in the plan this video keeps quoting. By then, about half of the coastal zone was public land, the plan says. Other families, after the Pfeiffers, had given land for parks too, and the plan credits their generosity.

Its basic rule was about what you can see. The county made it policy to prohibit all future development, public or private, visible from Highway 1 and from major public viewpoints. The plan calls everything in sight of those places the critical viewshed. It even names some of those viewpoints. One of them is the turnout at Bixby Creek, beside the bridge from the start of this video.

The test, in the plan's own words, was normal, unaided vision, in any direction, for any amount of time, at any season. If a new building would show, the plan says, it had to be moved, redesigned, or not built there at all. New roads and grading were not allowed to scar that view either.

Out of sight of the road, new homes were possible, with conditions. They had to go where the land or the trees would screen them. They couldn't sit on open hillsides, or on ridges against the sky.

The plan also treated the road itself as a limited resource. In 1986, it counted nearly three million visitors a year. Traffic jams on Highway 1 were already a problem, the plan says. It expected the number of visitors to double. So it reserved most of the highway's capacity for recreation and visitors. All the new homes together could use no more than 15 percent of it.

The rule didn't empty this coast. The coast was thinly settled long before 1986. What the plan decided was how the coast should look from the road, and who the road was for. In the 2020s, the trouble was keeping that road open at all.

So what happens to a coast like this when its road breaks? In January 2023, Paul's Slide closed Highway 1. In February 2024, Regent's Slide gave way, six miles to the north. Paul's Slide reopened that summer, but Regent's kept the road cut.

For almost three years, you couldn't drive this coast from end to end. Crews drilled thousands of steel bars into the slope at Regent's Slide to hold it in place. Caltrans reopened the road there at noon on January 14, 2026, months ahead of its target date. The agency estimated the repair at nearly 83 million dollars. Even then, it warned drivers to expect occasional full closures while crews cleared debris.

Fire was on the county's list of dangers, too. In August 2026, a wildfire started in the national forest above the coast. It became known as the Timber Fire, and it spread through these mountains. Air tankers from across California flew missions over the ridges. CAL FIRE, the state's fire agency, listed hundreds of homes, businesses and other buildings as threatened. Firefighters were hurt fighting it. By mid-October, it was almost fully contained.

For weeks, Caltrans kept parts of Highway 1 inside the census district closed. Farther south, a second fire, the Plaskett Fire, closed another stretch. For the people who live along this road, the fire came right after the long closures of the slides. By November 2026, the road was open from end to end again, with one-way traffic at a few work zones.

The census counted the homes along this road, too. In 2020, the census district had a little under 900 of them. Back in 1986, the county's plan had found homes like these in small clusters, or scattered along Highway 1. On census day in 2020, almost four in ten of the district's homes stood empty.

Empty, on census day, doesn't have to mean abandoned. The Census Bureau also runs a longer survey. Its results for 2020 to 2024 put nearly all of the district's empty homes in one category: seasonal, recreational or occasional use. In other words, they're homes people keep, but don't live in. Across California, homes like that make up only about a third of the empty ones.

The same 1986 plan described a serious housing shortage for the people who worked on this coast, especially in the visitor business. Some, it said, had camped out, lived in cars, or moved in with friends.

The visitors are the other side of the count. After the road reopened in 2026, Caltrans reported that the visitors came back. They come for the view the 1986 plan set out to protect. Then they drive on. The census doesn't count them, because this isn't where they live.

So how empty this coast looks depends on what you count. Count the people who live in the census district, and it's as empty as Wyoming. Count the homes, and many of them are kept by people who live somewhere else. Count the cars on Highway 1, and you find a road the county was already rationing in 1986.

Back at Bixby Creek, drivers pull into the turnout to look at the bridge from the start of this video. It's one of the viewpoints the county's rule was written to protect.

The creek below carries a homesteader's name. Above it runs a road that prisoners helped cut into the cliffs. Hardly a house is in sight. Part of that is the mountains, and part of it was a choice. In 1986, the county wrote that whatever came next should stay out of this view.

That highway runs all the way from one metro area to the other. Together, they hold more than 17 million people. In between, on census day, the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500 people who called it home.
